standard.title: Interaction skills and formality
standard.description: use interaction skills and awareness of formality when paraphrasing, questioning, clarifying and interrogating ideas, developing and supporting arguments, and sharing and evaluating information, experiences and opinions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use appropriate interaction skills including paraphrasing and questioning to clarify meaning and make connections to their own experiences (AC9E5LY02). They have not yet applied formality awareness to their interaction choices, or developed and supported arguments through structured oral exchange.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use interaction skills with awareness of formality across a range of spoken contexts — paraphrasing, questioning, clarifying, developing arguments, and sharing and evaluating ideas.

nodes.label: Formality in spoken interaction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can adapt their spoken interaction style to the level of formality required by the context.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least two different levels of formality in a spoken exchange; identify one language choice that signals the formality level.
nodes.typical_width: Participate in informal conversations, discussions and formal presentations; adjust vocabulary, tone and interaction style to match the formality of the context; identify when formality shifts are required.
wider: Participate in a formal debate or structured discussion and reflect on how formality requirements shaped language choices
Analyse a transcript of a formal vs. informal spoken exchange and identify the specific language features that signal each

response_modes.reason: Formality in spoken interaction requires practised flexibility — students who understand the concept of formality levels (AC9E6LA01) still need repeated spoken practice to deploy appropriate register naturally under the pressure of real-time interaction.

success_criteria: Uses language that consistently matches the expected formality level of the spoken context
Identifies at least one specific language choice made for formality reasons

nodes.label: Questioning and clarifying strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use paraphrasing, questioning, rephrasing and clarifying strategies purposefully in spoken interaction.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two questioning or clarifying strategies (e.g. paraphrasing, asking a clarifying question, rephrasing) in a discussion; explain why each was used.
nodes.typical_width: Use the full range of interaction strategies — pausing, questioning (open and closed), rephrasing, repeating, summarising, reviewing and asking clarifying questions — when discussing topics; recognise that closed questions ask for precise responses while open questions prompt elaboration.
wider: Analyse a recorded discussion and identify where different questioning strategies were used effectively and where missed opportunities for clarification occurred
Practise using open questions to probe and extend a speaker's ideas, and reflect on how this shapes the conversation

response_modes.reason: Students who have only practised paraphrasing and one type of questioning need to build a broader repertoire of interaction strategies before they can deploy them flexibly. Practice across multiple spoken contexts is the path to flexible, context-sensitive use.

success_criteria: Uses at least two distinct interaction strategies (e.g. open question, paraphrase, clarifying question) in a discussion
Explains the purpose of at least one strategy used

nodes.label: Developing and evaluating arguments in interaction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop and support arguments and share and evaluate information, experiences and opinions through spoken interaction.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least one argument orally and support it with a reason or evidence; evaluate one argument or opinion offered by another speaker.
nodes.typical_width: Develop, support and extend arguments in structured spoken contexts (discussions, debates); share and evaluate information, experiences and opinions using appropriate evidence and reasoning; interrogate ideas offered by others with relevant questions.
wider: Lead a structured group discussion on a topic, ensuring all participants contribute and arguments are developed and evaluated
Participate in a formal debate and reflect on how the structured format shaped argument development compared with informal discussion

response_modes.reason: Developing arguments in real-time spoken interaction requires integrating formality awareness (Node 1), questioning strategies (Node 2), and substantive content reasoning simultaneously — the coordination challenge is the learning.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Structured debate and discussion contexts are genuinely rich — they develop argument, reasoning, and civic participation skills that transfer across curriculum areas and into real-world communication contexts.
success_criteria: States an argument and supports it with at least one reason or piece of evidence
Evaluates at least one argument or opinion from another speaker, explaining whether and why they agree or disagree
